TEXAS (TX) — STATE CONTEXT MEMO
Litigation BD Targeting: Public School Districts
Prepared: September 1, 2026. All sources accessed September 1, 2026.
Assumed primary claim type: student-victim sexual abuse / failure-to-protect and failure-to-report claims against ISDs and charter schools, with secondary coverage of student transportation injury claims. Flag back if the target claim type differs — Texas immunity law is highly claim-specific and the analysis below does not transfer.

Not legal advice. Every item below should be re-verified against primary text before it is used in a pitch deck or demand letter.

---

1. LEGAL POSTURE — THE BASELINE (WHY TEXAS WAS HISTORICALLY A DEAD ZONE)

Texas school districts have enjoyed unusually broad tort immunity. 
Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.051 provides that, except as to motor vehicles, the Texas Tort Claims Act does not apply to a school district or junior college district.
 
The Texas Supreme Court has described the waiver for school districts as narrower than for other governmental units, encompassing only tort claims involving the use or operation of motor vehicles.
 
The premises/tangible-property portion of the Act does not reach school districts at all.


Individual staff are also shielded. 
Education Code § 22.0511 makes a professional employee not personally liable for acts incident to or within the scope of employment involving judgment or discretion, except where the employee uses excessive force in discipline or negligence results in bodily injury to students; the section does not apply to operation, use, or maintenance of a motor vehicle.


Practical read: pre-2025, viable state-law theories were essentially bus/vehicle cases. Institutional abuse claims were pushed into federal court (Title IX, § 1983/Monell) in the Fifth Circuit, a defense-favorable venue.

2. THE 2025 INFLECTION POINT — CPRC CHAPTER 118 (HB 4623)

This is the single most important development for BD targeting. 
Effective September 1, 2025, new Chapter 118 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code is described by the TASB Risk Management Fund as the first significant waiver of sovereign immunity for Texas public school districts since 1969.
 
Under Chapter 118, a district found grossly negligent in hiring, supervising, or employing a professional school employee who commits sexual abuse against a student, or who fails to report abuse or neglect, is liable for damages up to $500,000 for each claimant plus attorney fees and court costs.
 
TASB describes the standard as gross negligence, recklessness, or intentional misconduct in hiring, supervising, or employing; "professional school employee" is expanded to include teacher aides, substitute teachers, educator-preparation students in field placement, school bus drivers, and board members; governmental immunity is waived to the extent of liability, and the employee may not assert official immunity.
 
The individual employee must be named as a defendant, establishing joint and several liability between employee and school.
 
The enacted version eliminated exemplary damages.


Open item to verify before marketing: temporal reach. Chapter 118 is a new cause of action effective 9/1/2025; whether it reaches pre-effective-date conduct depends on the bill's transition language and is not resolved in the secondary sources reviewed. Do not represent retroactivity in any outreach until the enrolled bill text is confirmed.

3. DUTY ARCHITECTURE THAT GENERATES LIABILITY EVIDENCE (SB 571 / TEC CH. 22A)

Chapter 118 claims will be proved largely through breaches of the 2025 reporting regime. 
TEA states that SB 571 created Education Code Chapter 22A, requiring principals to report educator misconduct to the superintendent within 48 hours, superintendents to report qualifying allegations to TEA or SBEC within 48 hours, and all required misconduct reports to be submitted through the Misconduct Reporting Portal.
 
TASB notes the new requirements were effective for the 2025-2026 school year, and that a professional with reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused must report to DFPS or law enforcement within 24 hours.
 
Section 22A.151(b) mandates discharging or refusing to hire anyone on the Do Not Hire registry, and the registry is broader than a criminal history check.
 Legacy conduct is governed by the older regime: 
TEC § 22.093 (eff. 9/1/2019) required superintendents to report non-certified employees who resigned or were terminated amid evidence of abuse or a romantic/sexual relationship with a student, with reports due within seven business days
, and 
SB 7 (eff. 9/1/2017) amended TEC § 21.006 and added § 21.006(b-2), requiring principals to notify the superintendent no later than the seventh business day after obtaining certain information.


4. RECORDS RETENTION MECHANICS THAT MATTER FOR EVIDENCE

Governing schedule. 
TSLAC Local Schedule SD (Third Edition, effective May 23, 2018) establishes mandatory minimum retention periods for public school district records — including Part 7 Discipline and Counseling, Part 13 Transportation, Part 14 School Safety, and Part 16 Personnel and Staffing — and no local government office may dispose of a listed record before its retention period expires, nor adopt a shorter period.
 
Districts are also governed by Local Schedule GR (records common to all governments).
 
Districts typically designate the superintendent as Records Management Officer via TASB policy CPC(LOCAL), and must have a signed Form SLR 508 Declaration of Compliance on file.
